title: Equipment Lease Expenditures - Canadian SR&ED Glossary
description: Understand how Equipment Lease Expenditures are treated under Canadian SR&ED tax credit rules in our comprehensive R&D glossary.
summary: For Canadian SR&ED claimants, equipment lease and rental expenditures, such as cloud computing and software licences, cannot be claimed separately under the Proxy Method because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount already covers them; the Traditional Method allows directly related, incremental costs. Leasehold interests in buildings are excluded, while Saskatchewan's Budget 2026 added lease costs to its R&D credit.

Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Regime

Canada's primary fiscal mechanism for stimulating private-sector technological innovation is the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, which is codified within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Rather than operating as a discretionary subsidy or competitive grant, the federal SR&ED regime is an entitlement-based statutory framework administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada, which establishes legislative tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which executes technical and financial compliance, assessment, and audit verification. If a taxpayer's activities satisfy the statutory definition of eligible work and the associated outlays satisfy the legislative criteria for qualified expenditures, the resulting tax deductions and credits accrue by operation of law, provided all prescribed filing formalities are met within the statutory limitation period.
The Statutory Definition of SR&ED Under Subsection 248(1)

The legal threshold for determining whether commercial or industrial research activities qualify for tax incentives is anchored in the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. The statute defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. This overarching mandate is bifurcated into four eligible functional categories under paragraphs 248(1)(a) through (d) and bounded by seven explicit statutory exclusions under paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k).

Within the eligible categories, paragraph 248(1)(a) encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, whereas paragraph 248(1)(b) covers applied research, which is work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. In practice, the vast majority of Canadian corporate filings across industrial, manufacturing, software, and engineering sectors fall under paragraph 248(1)(c), which governs experimental development—work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Complementing these three core research pillars, paragraph 248(1)(d) admits eligible support work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, strictly to the extent that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development. Support work never qualifies on a standalone basis; its eligibility is entirely derivative of, and proportional to, an underlying core project under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c).

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the ITA explicitly exclude activities that, even when technically complex or commercially indispensable, do not constitute SR&ED. These statutorily excluded activities comprise market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection. Crucially, the CRA emphasizes in its administrative guidelines that achieving commercial novelty, product uniqueness, feature enhancement, or increased functionality does not, in itself, establish scientific or technological advancement under subsection 248(1) unless the work resolves an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be removed through standard practice or routine engineering.
The Two-Pronged Federal Incentive Mechanism

The federal SR&ED architecture delivers fiscal relief through a two-pronged statutory mechanism that separates the deduction of research expenses from the generation of tax credits. Under the first prong, governed by subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada in a taxation year may accumulate allowable SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada into a specialized Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures. This pool encompasses expenditures of a current nature under paragraph 37(1)(a) and—for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024—expenditures of a capital nature under paragraph 37(1)(b). The taxpayer may deduct any portion of the balance in the subsection 37(1) pool to reduce net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year or elect to carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Retaining an undeducted pool balance is a vital tax-planning instrument for pre-profit corporations seeking to preserve non-capital loss carryforwards that would otherwise expire after 20 years, as well as for corporations anticipating higher marginal corporate tax rates in subsequent fiscal periods.

Under the second prong, governed by subsections 127(5) and 127(9) and section 127.1 of the ITA, once an expenditure satisfies the requirements of section 37, it enters the calculation of the taxpayer's "qualified expenditure" and "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" under subsection 127(9). Based on this annual pool—which is computed at the end of each taxation year and does not carry over as an expenditure pool to subsequent years—the taxpayer earns SR&ED investment tax credits (ITCs). Depending on the taxpayer's legal classification, corporate control, taxable capital, and gross revenue, earned ITCs are utilized to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5) or refunded directly in cash as a "refundable investment tax credit" under section 127.1. Any non-refundable or unutilized portion of an SR&ED ITC may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset federal Part I tax payable. To prevent a double tax benefit from both deducting the full expenditure and receiving a tax credit on the same outlay, paragraph 12(1)(t) and paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA require that the amount of federal SR&ED ITC claimed by a taxpayer (whether refunded in cash or applied against tax payable) in a taxation year be recaptured into taxable income by reducing the taxpayer's subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the immediately following taxation year, with any excess over the available pool balance included directly in business income under paragraph 12(1)(t).
Transformational Legislative Reforms: Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026)

Following a decade of restrictive policy shifts initiated in the 2012 federal budget—which had reduced the basic ITC rate from 20% to 15%, lowered the prescribed proxy rate from 65% to 55%, restricted subcontractor inclusion to 80%, and repealed capital expenditure eligibility as of January 1, 2014—the Government of Canada enacted the most expansive modernization of the SR&ED regime in over a decade. Proposed across the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Federal Budget 2025, these legislative amendments were codified in Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026.

body.text: The enactment of Bill C-15 fundamentally alters corporate capital allocation across Canada's innovation ecosystem. Doubling the expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million eliminates the historical scaling cliff where mid-sized technology and life sciences ventures saw their marginal federal cash refund drop from 35% to 6% (40% of 15%)—or 0% if exceeding the qualifying income limit—once annual R&D spend crossed $3 million. Simultaneously, extending the 35% refundable rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) removes a major structural tax disincentive that previously penalized Canadian startups for listing on domestic public exchanges such as the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) or TSX Venture Exchange (TSXV), where going public immediately stripped the company of CCPC status and reduced its SR&ED benefit to a 15% non-refundable credit. Furthermore, providing CCPCs with an elective choice between the expanded $15 million–$75 million taxable capital phase-out and the new gross revenue phase-out ensures that capital-intensive clean-tech, semiconductor, and biotechnology ventures that raise large equity or debt rounds are not prematurely phased out of refundable credits before generating commercial revenues.
Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Entity Classifications, and Refundability Mechanics

The quantum and liquidity of federal SR&ED ITCs depend strictly on the legal classification of the claimant throughout the taxation year, its corporate association structure, and its prior-year capital or revenue metrics.
Qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs)

To qualify as a CCPC under subsection 125(7) and subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a corporation must be a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation and was not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (encompassing both de jure voting control and de facto control under subsection 256(5.1)), by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by a corporation with a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange, or by any combination thereof. CCPC status must be maintained throughout the entire taxation year; if a foreign acquirer or public parent gains control even on the final day of the fiscal year, CCPC status is forfeited for the entire taxation year.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a qualifying CCPC earns an enhanced ITC rate of 35% on its qualified SR&ED expenditures up to its annual Expenditure Limit, which reaches a maximum of $6,000,000. Under section 127.1 of the ITA, unused ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate by a qualifying CCPC (other than an excluded corporation) are 100% refundable in respect of qualified SR&ED expenditures of a current nature—generating a maximum annual cash refund of $2,100,000 ($6,000,000 multiplied by 35%)—and 40% refundable in respect of qualified SR&ED expenditures of a capital nature acquired after December 15, 2024.

Qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a CCPC in excess of its annual expenditure limit earn the basic ITC rate of 15%. If the CCPC qualifies as a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2)—meaning its taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year, combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations, did not exceed its qualifying income limit ($500,000, reduced proportionally as prior-year taxable capital rises above $15 million)—unused ITCs earned at the 15% basic rate on both current and capital expenditures are 40% refundable, yielding an effective cash refund of 6% (15% multiplied by 40%) of excess qualified expenditures. Where the CCPC exceeds its qualifying income limit, the 15% basic ITC is non-refundable.
Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas and Association Rules

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit is reduced for CCPCs whose taxable capital employed in Canada (as determined under Part I.3 of the ITA, sections 181.2 to 181.4, and reported on Schedule T2SCH33, T2SCH34, or T2SCH35) for the immediately preceding taxation year—aggregated across the claimant and all associated corporations—falls between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Prior to Bill C-15, the expenditure limit was governed by a dual reduction formula that phased out the $3 million limit based on both prior-year taxable income ($500,000 to $800,000) and prior-year taxable capital ($10 million to $50 million), before prior-year taxable income was removed from the federal expenditure limit grind (while being retained for the qualifying corporation 40% refundability test under subsection 127.1(2) and for Ontario's OITC).
Under the enacted post-December 15, 2024 taxable capital phase-out structure, the annual Expenditure Limit for an associated group is expressed mathematically as:

where TC represents the aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year. At TC ≤ $15,000,000, the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit is preserved; for every $10 of taxable capital above $15,000,000, the expenditure limit is reduced by $1, until it is completely eliminated at TC ≥ $75,000,000. Where a taxation year is shorter than 365 days (or 366 days in a leap year containing February 29), the expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365 (or 366).

Furthermore, under Bill C-15, a CCPC may elect out of the taxable capital phase-out structure and instead calculate its expenditure limit using the gross revenue phase-out structure established for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations. This election allows asset-heavy startups with substantial debt or share capital on their balance sheets (which inflates Part I.3 taxable capital above $15 million) but low commercial revenues to preserve their full $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit. When two or more corporations are associated with one another in a taxation year under section 256 of the ITA, they must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit and file an allocation agreement in prescribed form (Schedule T2SCH49) pursuant to subsection 127(10.3) of the ITA. Failure to account for corporate association—particularly across venture capital portfolio structures or founder holding companies—results in automated reassessment reducing the group's unallocated enhanced credit.
Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) are granted access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures annually (100% refundable on current expenditures and 40% refundable on capital expenditures), with a 15% non-refundable basic ITC on qualified expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 limit. To qualify as an ECPC, a corporation must be a resident of Canada, have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or have elected to be a public corporation), and must not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons. Unlike CCPCs, an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out strictly based on its average gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (aggregated across corporate group members on a consolidated basis) rather than Part I.3 taxable capital.
Foreign-Controlled Subsidiaries, Non-Qualifying Public Corporations, and Unincorporated Entities

Canadian subsidiaries controlled by foreign parent corporations (such as United States, European, or Asian multinationals), public corporations exceeding the gross revenue phase-out ceiling, and CCPCs with prior-year taxable capital of $75 million or more (that do not qualify under the gross revenue election) earn the basic ITC rate of 15% on all qualified SR&ED expenditures. For these corporations, the 15% federal ITC is strictly non-refundable; it may only be applied to reduce federal Part I income tax otherwise payable in the current year, carried back 3 taxation years, or carried forward 20 taxation years.

Unincorporated individuals (sole proprietorships) and trusts carrying on a business in Canada also earn the basic ITC rate of 15% on qualified SR&ED expenditures. Under section 127.1 of the ITA, unused ITCs earned by individuals and trusts at the 15% rate are 40% refundable in cash (resulting in a 6% immediate cash refund and a 9% non-refundable credit available for carryback or carryforward), claimed via Form T2038(IND). By contrast, because a partnership is not a separate taxable person under subsection 96(1) of the ITA, a partnership does not earn or claim SR&ED tax credits directly on a corporate or individual return. Instead, SR&ED expenditures are deducted at the partnership level in computing partnership net income for the fiscal period, and the resulting ITC is calculated at the partnership level and allocated to eligible members in accordance with their respective partnership interests under subsection 127(8). Limited partners (other than general partners) are statutorily barred from being allocated SR&ED ITCs, and partnership expenditures do not qualify for the 35% enhanced CCPC rate unless flowed through specific corporate partner rules.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methodologies, and Statutory Reductions

Under subsections 37(1), 37(8), and 127(9) of the ITA and section 2900 of the ITR, only specific categories of expenditures incurred in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada (and limited foreign salary outlays) enter the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool and the qualified expenditure pool for ITC calculation.
Salaries and Wages: Direct Labour, Foreign Work, and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages—including the employer's share of statutory payroll contributions such as Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Employment Insurance (EI), provincial health taxes, and workers' compensation—paid to employees for the portion of their time directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada are 100% includable in both the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) ITC pool. Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, whether an employee is "directly engaged" is determined by the technical nature of the tasks performed rather than the employee's formal job title; hands-on experimentation, coding, prototype fabrication, testing, and direct first-line technical supervision of ongoing experiments qualify, whereas general administrative duties, human resources, finance, and high-level executive oversight do not. Where an employee spends all or substantially all (90% or more) of their working time in the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be claimed.
Permissible SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (Subsection 37(1.4))

While section 37 generally restricts tax incentives to SR&ED carried on within the geographic boundaries of Canada (including Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone), subsection 37(1.4) provides a narrow statutory exception for salaries or wages paid to a Canadian resident employee for SR&ED performed outside Canada. To qualify under subsection 37(1.4), the foreign work must be an integral part of, and solely in support of, a core SR&ED project carried on in Canada by the taxpayer, and the remuneration must not be subject to foreign income or profits tax. The total amount of foreign SR&ED salaries and wages claimable under subsection 37(1.4) is strictly capped at 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada during the taxation year. Foreign subcontractor fees, materials consumed abroad, and foreign overhead remain 100% excluded.
Specified Employees: Statutory Caps Under Subsection 37(9.1) and Regulations 2900(7)–(8)

Stringent statutory anti-avoidance limits apply to specified employees to prevent owner-managers from extracting corporate profits as tax-subsidized R&D bonuses. Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" of the employer—defined as a person who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, not less than 10% of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of any corporation related to the corporation (counting shares owned by persons with whom the employee does not deal at arm's length)—or who otherwise does not deal at arm's length with the employer.

For a specified employee, two distinct statutory caps govern eligible remuneration. First, under the Direct Salary Cap in subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, all bonuses and remuneration based on profits are 100% excluded from a specified employee's SR&ED salary claim. Furthermore, the maximum deductible and ITC-eligible SR&ED salary or wages for a specified employee cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee. For the 2026 taxation year, the CPP YMPE is $74,600.00, establishing a maximum direct SR&ED salary cap of $373,000 per specified employee. If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, the 5× YMPE limit must be allocated among the associated employers using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)).

Second, under the Proxy Salary Base Cap in subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the ITR, when the claimant elects to use the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method to calculate overhead, the amount of a specified employee's salary that can enter the proxy salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 is restricted to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits under sections 6 and 7 of the ITA) and 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was employed by the taxpayer in the year. For the 2026 taxation year, this 2.5× YMPE proxy salary base ceiling equals $186,500. Expressed mathematically, the maximum proxy salary base contribution for a specified employee is:
Proxy salary base contribution = min(SR&ED salary; 75% × S; 2.5 × YMPE × D ÷ 365)

where the first term is the specified employee's direct SR&ED salary (already capped at 5 × YMPE), S is their total base salary excluding bonuses and taxable benefits, and D is the number of days employed in the taxation year.
Overhead Calculation Methodologies: Prescribed Proxy Amount vs. Traditional Method

In Part 3, Section A (Line 160/162) of Form T661, a claimant must elect annually between two mutually exclusive methodologies for claiming SR&ED overhead and other expenditures: the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method (also referred to as the Proxy Method) or the Traditional Method. Under paragraph 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA, this election is irrevocable for the taxation year once Form T661 is filed; a taxpayer cannot amend its return to switch from the proxy method to the traditional method (or vice versa) for that fiscal year.
The Prescribed Proxy Amount (Proxy Method — Regulation 2900(4))

Under the Proxy Method, the taxpayer does not specifically identify, track, or deduct actual SR&ED overhead costs in the subsection 37(1) pool; instead, overhead costs such as rent, utilities, office supplies, and general support staff are deducted as ordinary business expenses under section 9 and paragraph 18(1)(a) of the ITA. In lieu of actual overhead, the taxpayer computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations equal to 55% of the eligible salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada. Practitioners must note that while the PPA rate was 65% for taxation years ending before 2013 and 60% prorated for 2013, it has remained fixed at 55% since January 1, 2014.

Under Regulation 2900(9), the proxy salary base (calculated in Part 5, Section A of Form T661) strictly excludes, for all employees (both arm's-length and specified employees), bonuses and remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits conferred under section 6 (such as automobile benefits or group term life insurance) or section 7 (employee stock options) of the ITA, employer contributions to registered pension plans, CPP, EI, or workers' compensation boards, and unpaid salary amounts deemed not incurred under subsection 78(4). The resulting 55% PPA is entered on Line 502 in Part 4 of Form T661, where it increases the "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" for ITC calculation purposes only. Consequently, for a qualifying CCPC claiming an arm's-length software engineer's base salary of $100,000 spent 100% on SR&ED in Canada, the qualified expenditure is $155,000 ($100,000 + 55% × $100,000), yielding a federal refundable ITC (before provincial assistance grinds) of $54,250 ($155,000 × 35%), or an effective federal recovery of 54.25% of direct base salary.
The Traditional Method and the Treatment of Cloud Computing and SaaS Costs

Under the Traditional Method, governed by subparagraph 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the ITA and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the ITR, the taxpayer foregoes the 55% notional proxy and instead itemizes and substantiates actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. To qualify under the Traditional Method, each overhead outlay must be directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—meaning the expense would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not been carried out—or be prescribed overhead directly attributable to SR&ED under Regulation 2900.

A critical audit flashpoint in modern technology claims involves cloud computing infrastructure (such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud GPU clusters) and Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) or CAD subscriptions. Under the Proxy Method, cloud computing invoices, SaaS development environment subscriptions, and software licences cannot be claimed separately. They are classified by the CRA as overhead or rental/lease expenditures that are already notionally represented by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount; attempting to claim cloud computing costs as "materials consumed" or "subcontractors" while electing the Proxy Method is a major audit error that results in automatic disallowance. Conversely, under the Traditional Method, incremental cloud computing and server hosting expenses dedicated specifically to training experimental artificial intelligence models, running computational fluid dynamics simulations, or hosting isolated R&D test environments can be claimed as directly related and incremental overhead, provided the taxpayer maintains granular telemetry or billing logs segregating R&D compute instances from commercial production servers. Thus, for compute-intensive AI startups where incremental GPU cloud spend exceeds 55% of the direct SR&ED salary base, electing the Traditional Method yields a substantially higher ITC than the Proxy Method.

body.text: Materials Consumed or Transformed and ITC Recapture Rules

Under clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II) of the ITA, a taxpayer may claim 100% of the cost of materials that are either consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed (reported on Line 320 of Form T661) encompass items that are destroyed, rendered virtually valueless, or exhausted during experimentation or testing, such as chemical reagents, laboratory consumables, and destructive testing specimens. Materials transformed (reported on Line 325 of Form T661) comprise materials that are integrated into a prototype, pilot plant, custom product, or experimental production run where the resulting item retains potential commercial value at the conclusion of the experiment.

When materials are transformed into a property—or when capital equipment is claimed for SR&ED—and that property is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the ITC recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(34) of the ITA are triggered. Under subsection 127(27), if within 20 taxation years of acquiring the property the taxpayer disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use, the taxpayer must add back ("recapture") directly to its federal Part I tax payable for that year an amount equal to the lesser of the SR&ED ITC originally earned in respect of the particular property (or materials incorporated into the property) and the amount determined by multiplying the historical ITC percentage rate used when the credit was earned by either the proceeds of disposition of the property (if sold to an arm's-length party) or the fair market value of the property at the time of conversion (if converted to commercial use or transferred to a non-arm's length party). Parallel recapture provisions apply to non-arm's length transfers of qualified expenditures under subsection 127(29) and non-arm's length dispositions under subsection 127(34).
Contract Expenditures (Subcontractors) and Third-Party Payments

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, payments made by a claimant for SR&ED performed on its behalf in Canada by an arm's-length contractor that is a "taxable supplier" (generally a Canadian resident person or Canadian partnership, or a non-resident operating through a Canadian permanent establishment) qualify as SR&ED contract expenditures. While 100% of an eligible arm's-length contract expenditure is deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool, only 80% of the contract expenditure is included in the "qualified expenditure" pool for ITC calculation purposes. This 20% statutory reduction, enacted effective January 1, 2013, is designed to strip out the contractor's embedded profit margin so that ITCs are not paid on commercial markups. Consequently, for a qualifying CCPC earning the 35% enhanced ITC, an arm's-length Canadian subcontractor invoice of $100,000 yields a federal credit of $28,000 ($100,000 × 80% × 35%), representing an effective 28% federal credit rate.

Under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, where an arm's-length contract involves SR&ED performed on the payer's behalf, both the payer and the contractor may appear to have a claim unless properly coordinated through the contract payment rules. Furthermore, if the contract is with a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier (for instance, a foreign contractor performing work without a Canadian permanent establishment), 80% of the amount is subtracted on Line 528 of Form T661, reducing the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to nil.

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1) of the ITA, third-party payments made by a taxpayer to an approved association, university, college, research institute, or non-profit R&D corporation (exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j) of the ITA) for SR&ED carried on in Canada—where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results of that SR&ED in its business—are similarly 100% deductible under subsection 37(1) and included at 80% for ITC purposes. Each third-party payment must be reported on Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)). Conversely, under subsection 37(14) (the look-through rule) and the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), an expenditure paid by a claimant to a person or partnership with whom the claimant does not deal at arm's length (as defined in section 251 of the ITA) for the performance of SR&ED is excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures. Instead, the non-arm's length performer incurs the qualified expenditures directly on its underlying labour, materials, and overhead, and may optionally transfer up to the contract amount of those qualified expenditures to the non-arm's length payer by jointly executing and filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) pursuant to subsections 127(13) and 127(14) of the ITA.
Restored Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

Reversing the 11-year exclusion that took effect on January 1, 2014, Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III), subsection 127(9), and paragraph 2902(b) of the Income Tax Regulations for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). To qualify as an All or Substantially All (ASA) SR&ED Capital Expenditure, the asset must be new depreciable property (for which Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) could otherwise be claimed under paragraph 20(1)(a) of the ITA) owned by the claimant (or in which the claimant holds a qualifying leasehold interest, other than in a building) and must satisfy one of two intent tests at the time of acquisition: either the property is intended to be used during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada, or all or substantially all (90% or more) of the property's value is intended to be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada.

Eligible capital assets include dedicated R&D laboratory instruments, environmental test chambers, specialized prototyping machinery, custom experimental tooling and moulds, and dedicated research computer hardware. When an ASA capital expenditure is claimed under paragraph 37(1)(b), 100% of its capital cost is immediately deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool (in lieu of regular CCA) and enters the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for ITC calculation, earning 35% for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit (with 40% refundability) or the 15% basic ITC.

For new depreciable machinery and equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the strict 90% ASA threshold, but is used primarily (more than 50%) of its operating time for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, the restored Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) rules under subsection 127(9) ("first term shared-use-equipment" and "second term shared-use-equipment") and Regulation 2900(11) apply. Under the SUE rules, up to 50% of the capital cost of the equipment qualifies for SR&ED ITCs, claimed in two equal tranches: 25% of the capital cost at the end of the "first term" (minimum 12 months after acquisition and available-for-use) and 25% at the end of the "second term" (minimum 24 months after acquisition), provided primary (>50%) SR&ED usage is maintained throughout each term.

Several statutory exclusions and timing rules govern capital property claims. Under paragraph 37(8)(d) of the ITA and paragraph 2902(b) of the ITR, land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are strictly excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures, even if a specialized cleanroom or test facility is constructed. Used depreciable property may qualify for the subsection 37(1)(b) income tax deduction pool if it meets the 90% ASA test, but is excluded under Regulation 2902(b) from earning SR&ED ITCs. Furthermore, while paragraph 37(1)(b) applies to capital expenditures made after December 15, 2024, subsection 127(11.2) of the ITA (as amended by Bill C-15) deems capital property not to have been acquired for ITC purposes until it becomes "available for use" by the taxpayer within the meaning of subsections 13(26) to 13(32) of the ITA. Consequently, equipment ordered or paid for prior to December 16, 2024, that only became delivered, installed, and available for use on or after December 16, 2024, triggers specific timing interactions under subsection 127(11.2) for ITC eligibility.
Unpaid Amounts (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26))

To prevent accrual-basis taxpayers from claiming cash tax refunds on expenses that remain unpaid indefinitely, the ITA enforces strict 180-day payment rules. Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any SR&ED salary, wage, or accrued remuneration that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year, and is instead deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (reported on Lines 310 and 315 of Form T661). If an accrued bonus to a specified employee is caught by subsection 78(4), it remains permanently ineligible for SR&ED even when paid, as bonuses are excluded for specified employees. Similarly, under subsection 127(26) of the ITA, any current SR&ED expenditure other than salary or wages (such as arm's-length subcontractor invoices, materials, or traditional overhead) that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year remains in the subsection 37(1) deduction pool (unless subject to general subsection 78(1) non-arm's length unpaid rules), but is excluded from qualified expenditures for ITC purposes on Line 520 of Form T661 until the taxation year in which it is actually paid.
Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), and 127(19) of the ITA, both the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes must be reduced by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment in respect of SR&ED that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year.

Government assistance is defined in subsection 127(9) as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or in any other form, other than a federal SR&ED ITC. This encompasses direct federal and provincial innovation grants—such as National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) contributions, Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) grants, Scale AI reimbursements, AI Compute Access Fund subsidies, and Regional AI Initiative (RAII) interest-free loan benefits—as well as all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and grants (including the Ontario OITC and ORDTC, Quebec CRIC, Alberta IEG, and BC SR&ED credit) and Mitacs or Student Work Placement Program (SWPP) wage subsidies, including funding channeled through non-profit entities funded by government. Non-government assistance includes inducements, reimbursements, or contributions received from private-sector or non-governmental entities that would otherwise be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) of the ITA.

A contract payment is defined in subsection 127(9) as an amount paid or payable to a claimant by an arm's-length "taxable supplier" for SR&ED performed "for, or on behalf of," a person or partnership entitled to a deduction under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) or (i.1), or an amount payable by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity (under section 149) for SR&ED performed for it or on its behalf. Where a project's assistance and contract payments exceed the project's SR&ED expenditures, subsection 127(19) transfers the excess reduction to any non-arm's length party performing work on that same project; to allocate assistance among non-arm's length group members, claimants must file Form T1145. Conversely, when a taxpayer repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its SR&ED pools (such as repaying a conditional government contribution), the repayment restores the deductible pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and generates ITC additions under subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8), reported on Line 560 of Form T661.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal Grind Mechanics

Every Canadian province (with the exception of Prince Edward Island) and the Yukon Territory supplements the federal SR&ED program with its own sub-national R&D tax credit or tax-system grant. While the majority of provinces harmonize their definition of eligible SR&ED with subsection 248(1) of the federal ITA and delegate administration to the CRA via schedules attached to the federal T2 return, Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration) operate autonomous, standalone regimes with independent filing forms and expenditure rules.
Mathematical Mechanics of the "Federal Grind" (Assistance Reduction)

Because provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and grants constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(18) of the federal ITA, the provincial credit earned in respect of a taxation year (reported on Line 513 of federal Form T661) reduces dollar-for-dollar the federal qualified expenditure pool on which the federal SR&ED ITC is computed. Consequently, the combined federal-provincial credit rate on a given dollar of qualified SR&ED expenditure is not the simple arithmetic sum of the federal rate and the provincial rate, but is governed by the multiplicative formula:
Combined rate = P + F × (1 − P), where P is the provincial credit rate and F is the federal ITC rate

To illustrate this interaction, in a jurisdiction offering a 15% refundable provincial R&D tax credit (such as Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, or Yukon) stacked with the 35% federal enhanced CCPC rate on $1,000,000 of qualified current expenditures, the corporation first earns a provincial R&D credit of $150,000 ($1,000,000 multiplied by 15%) in refundable cash. That $150,000 provincial credit reduces the federal qualified expenditure base to $850,000 ($1,000,000 minus $150,000), on which the 35% federal enhanced ITC generates $297,500 ($850,000 multiplied by 35%) in refundable federal cash. The combined total cash refund equals $447,500 ($150,000 plus $297,500), representing an effective combined rate of 44.75% of qualified expenditures rather than 50%. When applied to $1,000,000 of direct Canadian SR&ED base salaries utilizing the 55% federal and provincial proxy overhead ($1,550,000 of qualified expenditures), the combined cash refund reaches $693,625 ($1,550,000 multiplied by 44.75%), or 69.36% of direct SR&ED payroll.
Comprehensive Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Comparison

body.text: Deep-Dive Analysis of Key Provincial Regimes
Quebec: Transition from Legacy RD-1029.7 to the Modernized CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025)

Quebec administers its R&D tax incentives independently through Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Quebec). In the March 2025 Quebec Budget Plan, the Quebec Ministry of Finance enacted a sweeping structural consolidation, replacing eight separate legacy R&D and innovation tax credits—most notably the flagship Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) claimed on Form RD-1029.7—with a single unified regime: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC).

For all taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, corporations are legally barred from filing Form RD-1029.7—which Revenu Québec automatically rejects for post-March 25, 2025 fiscal periods—and must claim exclusively under the CRIC regime. For taxation years that began on or before March 25, 2025, claimants file under the legacy Form RD-1029.7 rules, where eligible R&D salaries and 50% of subcontractor outlays were subject to an asset-based exclusion threshold scaling linearly from $50,000 (for corporations with total assets of $1 million or less) to $225,000 (for corporations with total assets of $12.5 million or more).

Under the modernized CRIC regime, the credit is 100% refundable for every corporation carrying on R&D in Quebec, regardless of whether the claimant is a CCPC, a public corporation, or a foreign-controlled multinational subsidiary. The CRIC provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified R&D expenditures exceeding the corporation's exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable credit on all qualified R&D expenditures above that $1,000,000 tier. Under CRIC, the legacy asset-based exclusion threshold is replaced by a simplified exclusion threshold equal to the greater of a $50,000 base floor or $18,571 per employee who devotes time to R&D activities, prorated by the proportion of working time spent on R&D. Arm's-length Quebec subcontractor payments are included in the CRIC base at 50%.
Ontario: Dual Stacking of OITC and ORDTC and Capital Expenditure Rules

Ontario corporations benefit from two primary general R&D tax credits administered by the CRA, which can be claimed concurrently on the same underlying Ontario SR&ED expenditures in addition to the 20% refundable Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) for university and research institute contracts. The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC, claimed on Schedule 566) provides an 8% refundable tax credit to CCPCs on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, generating a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000. Crucially, Ontario has only partially harmonized with the federal Bill C-15 expansion: Ontario's OITC expenditure limit remains capped at $3,000,000 rather than the new $6,000,000 federal limit and continues to phase out when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or prior-year taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. By contrast, capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 are eligible for both the OITC and the ORDTC, a change that took effect in Ontario automatically when the corresponding federal legislation in Bill C-15 was enacted.

Alongside the OITC, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC, claimed on Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations (both CCPCs and non-CCPCs) with a permanent establishment in Ontario. Because the OITC itself is government assistance that reduces the eligible expenditure pool for the ORDTC, a qualifying CCPC claiming both OITC (8%) and ORDTC (3.5%) on $100,000 of Ontario expenditures earns $8,000 of OITC, which reduces the ORDTC base to $92,000 and yields $3,220 ($92,000 multiplied by 3.5%) of ORDTC, unless the corporation elects to waive or renounce the non-refundable ORDTC to prevent it from grinding down the 35% refundable federal ITC.
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), Base-Spend Mechanics, and the Bill C-15 Line 557 Rule

Alberta operates a standalone corporate tax system administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA). Effective January 1, 2021, Alberta replaced its former provincial SR&ED credit with the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), which is claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) alongside the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1). Under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and Information Circular IEG-1R4, the IEG rewards corporations that grow their Alberta R&D footprint through a two-part calculation up to a $4,000,000 annual expenditure limit. Under Part I (the 8% Base Payment), the corporation earns 8% on the lesser of its current-year eligible Alberta R&D expenditures (Line 031 of Form AT29) and its $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit (Line 108). Under Part II (the 12% Incremental Bonus, creating a 20% total rate), the corporation earns an additional 12% on the amount by which the lesser of its current-year eligible expenditures and $4,000,000 exceeds its "Base Amount" (Line 118), where the Base Amount is defined as the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta R&D expenditures for the two immediately preceding taxation years. Consequently, a first-time R&D claimant in Alberta (or a company with $0 Alberta R&D spend in the prior two years) has a Base Amount of $0 and earns the full 20% refundable IEG rate (8% plus 12%) on 100% of its eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to $4,000,000.

The IEG is available to all corporations (not restricted to CCPCs), but phases out linearly for corporations (and associated groups) whose prior-year federal taxable capital employed in Canada (from Line 690 of federal Schedule T2SCH33) lies between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, governed by the multiplier on Line 128 of Form AT29:
Line 128 multiplier = ($50,000,000 − TC) ÷ $40,000,000, where 0 ≤ multiplier ≤ 1 and TC is prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada

Corporations with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital receive no IEG. Furthermore, because the Alberta proxy amount (Line 009 of Form AT29, calculated at 55% of the Alberta salary base) and eligible expenditures depend on federal Form T661, and the resulting IEG must be reported as provincial government assistance on Line 513 of federal Form T661, TRA mandates a two-step iterative calculation in the Guide to Claiming the Innovation Employment Grant. In Step 1, the claimant calculates the initial IEG on Form AT29 before deducting the IEG as provincial government assistance on federal Form T661. In Step 2, the claimant enters the Step 1 IEG amount on Line 513 of federal Form T661, recalculates the federal qualified expenditure amounts, and feeds the updated federal figure back into Form AT29 to determine the final net IEG (Line 134 of Form AT29, carried to Line 129 of the AT1 return). Crucially, following the enactment of federal Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, Alberta TRA updated AT1 Schedule 29 to prevent restored federal capital expenditures from entering the Alberta IEG calculation: for taxation years ending before December 16, 2024, Form AT29 pulls from Line 559 of federal Form T661 (total SR&ED qualified expenditure pool), whereas for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, Form AT29 strictly pulls from Line 557 of federal Form T661 (current SR&ED expenditures only), excluding capital expenditures reported on Line 558.
Governing Bodies, Prescribed Filing Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Administration
Administrative Architecture of the CRA SR&ED Directorate

Within the Canada Revenue Agency, the SR&ED program is administered through specialized Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs) located across Canada. When an SR&ED claim is filed with a Tax Centre, automated risk-scoring algorithms—augmented since April 2026 by the CRA's expanded artificial intelligence risk-assessment framework announced in Budget 2025—evaluate whether the claim should be accepted as filed or routed to a CTSO for a desk review or detailed field audit. Claims selected for detailed review at a CTSO are evaluated by two distinct functional specialists: a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), who is a domain-qualified scientist, engineer, or computer scientist tasked with evaluating Part 2 of Form T661 and contemporaneous technical evidence to determine whether the claimed projects satisfy subsection 248(1) of the ITA, and a Financial Reviewer (FR), who is a tax auditor tasked with examining Parts 3 through 6 of Form T661, payroll ledgers, time-tracking records, subcontractor contracts, and proof of payment to verify compliance with sections 37 and 127 of the ITA and section 2900 of the ITR.
Line-by-Line Architecture of Form T661 and Prescribed Schedules

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA, a taxpayer cannot deduct an SR&ED expenditure or earn an SR&ED ITC unless it files the prescribed form containing the prescribed information. The foundational prescribed document for all claimants is Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), interpreted alongside CRA Guide T4088 (Guide to Form T661). In its 2026 revision, Form T661 was expanded to incorporate separate reporting columns for current expenditures, restored post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures, and shared-use equipment.

cells: Claimant name (Line 010), 15-character Business Number (BN), tax year dates, total number of projects claimed (Line 050), financial contact (Lines 100–110), technical contact (Lines 115–125), and partnership details (Lines 151–157).
Project Information (Sections A, B, and C — Lines 200 to 282)

Section A: Project title, field of science/technology code, continuation status, start/completion dates. Section B: Technical narratives addressing technological uncertainties (Line 242, max 350 words), work performed / systematic investigation (Line 244, max 700 words), and technological advancements (Line 246, max 350 words). Section C: Contemporaneous evidence checklist and personnel/contractor indicators. Rule on 20 Largest Projects: Claimants may submit Part 2 upon filing for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, but must complete and retain Part 2 for all projects at their place of business to provide upon CRA request.
Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures (Sections A, B, and C — Lines 160 to 460)

Section A: Irrevocable annual election between the Proxy Method and Traditional Method. Section B: Calculation of allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures (salaries/wages, subsection 78(4) unpaid adjustments, materials consumed on Line 320 and transformed on Line 325, arm's-length and NAL contracts, third-party payments, traditional overhead on Line 360). Section C: Calculation of the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (government/non-government assistance deductions, prior-year ITC recapture, repayments on Line 445, current-year deduction claimed on Line 460, and carryforward balance).
Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Lines 492 to 560)

Segregates current and capital expenditures; adds the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Line 502; applies the 80% inclusion rule to arm's-length contracts and third-party payments; deducts provincial government assistance on Line 513 and other assistance/contract payments; deducts unpaid amounts under subsection 127(26) on Line 520 and payments to non-taxable suppliers on Line 528; outputs current qualified expenditures (Line 557), capital qualified expenditures (Line 558), total SR&ED qualified expenditure pool (Line 559), and assistance repayments (Line 560).
Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) (Sections A and B)

Section A: Computes the eligible salary base under Regulation 2900(9) and applies the specified employee caps (lesser of 75% of total salary or 2.5× YMPE under Regulations 2900(7)–(8)). Section B: Applies the 55% proxy rate (subject to overall salary/overhead cap rules) to determine the PPA transferred to Line 502.
Mandatory project-by-project cost allocation matrix detailing salaries, materials, and contract costs for every SR&ED project claimed in the year (even if more than 20 projects are claimed).
Statistical breakdown of SR&ED expenditures by source of funds, country, province/territory, and field of science code.

Mandatory disclosure under subsection 162(5.1) of every external claim preparer who accepted consideration to prepare or assist with the claim, including preparer BN/SIN, fee structure (contingency vs. fixed/hourly), and total fee paid.
Signature and certification by an authorized signing officer of the claimant.

body.text: In addition to Form T661, a claimant must file the appropriate ITC calculation schedule and any applicable ancillary forms: Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporate claimants, or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) for unincorporated individuals and trusts; Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), which was updated in 2026 to break down allocated assistance between current expenditures on Line 015 and capital expenditures on Line 020; Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), which was similarly updated in 2026 to separate transferred current expenditures on Line 015 and capital expenditures on Line 020; Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED); and Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED).
The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Bar (Subsections 37(11), 127(9)(m), and 220(2.2))

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA, the prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information in respect of each project and expenditure must be filed with the Minister of National Revenue on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date under subsection 150(1) for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. For corporations, paragraph 150(1)(a) establishes a T2 income tax return filing-due date of 6 months after the end of the taxation year; adding 12 months creates an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of 18 months after the end of the corporation's taxation year (for example, a corporation with a December 31, 2025 taxation year-end has a T2 filing-due date of June 30, 2026, and an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of June 30, 2027). For unincorporated individuals carrying on a business in the year, the T1 return filing-due date is June 15 of the following calendar year, establishing an SR&ED reporting deadline of June 15 of the second following calendar year (17.5 months after the December 31 year-end). For trusts, paragraph 150(1)(c) sets the T3 return filing-due date at 90 days after the taxation year-end, establishing an SR&ED reporting deadline of 15 months (90 days plus 12 months) after the trust's year-end.

Unlike general tax elections that qualify for late-filing relief under the taxpayer relief provisions of subsection 220(3.2) or ministerial discretion to waive filing requirements under subsection 220(2.1), subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA explicitly strips the Minister of National Revenue (and the Tax Court of Canada) of any legal authority to extend the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline. If a corporation files Form T661 or Schedule T2SCH31 even one day after the 18-month deadline (unless the deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday, in which case the Interpretation Act extends it to the next business day), or attempts to amend a timely filed Form T661 after the 18-month deadline expires to increase an expenditure line or add an omitted project, the claim or additional expenditure is permanently and irrevocably statute-barred. Only two narrow statutory mechanics fall outside the 18-month bar: deducting an amount from a previously identified subsection 37(1) pool carryforward balance, and amending Part 9 claim preparer information.
The New Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and CRA Service Standards

Historically, the CRA offered non-binding educational and advisory programs, including the Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT), the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS), the Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC), and the Pre-Claim Review (PCR), which had replaced the earlier Pre-Claim Project Review (PCPR). While useful for claimant orientation, those legacy services did not provide a multi-year binding technical approval integrated with a fast-track refund processing standard.

As announced in Federal Budget 2025 and confirmed in the 2026 Spring Economic Update, on April 1, 2026, the CRA officially launched the Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process, allowing eligible businesses to secure a formal, up-front technical determination on planned or in-progress R&D projects before filing their tax return. Participation in the Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process is open to Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), other Canadian corporations, and partnerships that are in good standing with the CRA and have annual gross business income of less than $25,000,000. The application must cover new work only—meaning projects that have not previously appeared in an SR&ED claim—and is capped at a maximum of 3 projects per request.

To initiate the process, the business requests a case number from the CRA, completes the technical project application (structured similarly to Part 2 of Form T661), and uploads it through My Business Account. Within 4 weeks of submission, the claimant's technical lead meets with a CRA SR&ED Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) for a structured 2-to-5-hour technical meeting. The CRA issues a formal written technical eligibility decision within 8 weeks of receiving a complete application. Once granted, a pre-claim project approval remains valid for up to 3 years, providing multi-year technical certainty across consecutive fiscal filings.

The CRA's standard service timelines for post-filing SR&ED claims are 60 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim for refundable claims accepted as filed without audit review, 180 calendar days for refundable claims selected for technical and/or financial review, and 365 calendar days for non-refundable claims selected for review. Under the April 1, 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process, if a refundable claim is selected for an expenditure review and contains only projects that received pre-claim approval (without material divergence from the approved scope), the CRA's processing timeline is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days. However, if a claimant bundles even a single unapproved project (or a project whose executed scope materially differs from the approved submission) alongside pre-approved projects in the same annual Form T661 filing, the entire claim reverts to the standard 180-day review track. Moreover, pre-claim approval confers technical project approval only; the CRA retains full authority to audit the financial quantum and substantiation of the claimed expenditures during the 90-day window.
Dispute Resolution: Administrative Second Review, Notice of Objection, and Tax Court Appeal

When a CTSO review results in a negative eligibility or financial proposal, the CRA's dispute resolution framework proceeds through four sequential stages. First, during informal resolution following a site visit or review, the RTA and FR issue a draft SR&ED Review Report and proposal letter, affording the claimant a response window (typically 30 days) to submit rebuttal evidence directly to the RTA/FR and, if unresolved, to escalate to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) or Financial Review Manager (FRM). Second, if managerial discussions do not resolve the dispute and the claimant believes the review process failed to adhere to due process or administrative fairness, the claimant may request an Administrative Second Review conducted by the Assistant Director, SR&ED at the CTSO prior to the issuance of a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment. Third, once a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the taxpayer has 90 days from the date of mailing of the notice (under section 165 of the ITA) to file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA's independent Appeals Branch, which assigns an Appeals Officer (and an independent Appeals Technical Advisor) to conduct a de novo administrative review. Fourth, if the CRA Appeals Branch confirms or varies the reassessment (or if 90 days have elapsed after filing the Notice of Objection without a decision by the Minister), the taxpayer may file a Notice of Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada under section 169 of the ITA, whose judgments may subsequently be appealed on questions of law to the Federal Court of Appeal.
Judicial Precedents, Case Law Evolution, and Statutory Penalty Regimes
Foundational Jurisprudence: The Northwest Hydraulic Five-Question Test

The bedrock of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence is the landmark decision of Judge Donald Bowman (as he then was, later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (Tax Court of Canada, Docket 97-531-IT-G, decided May 1, 1998). Interpreting the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA and reviewing CRA Information Circular 86-4R3 (dated May 24, 1994), Judge Bowman articulated the canonical five-criterion judicial test for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED.

Under the first question, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Judge Bowman defined "routine engineering" as techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field; if the resolution of a problem is reasonably predictable using established engineering methodologies, no technological uncertainty exists, even if the design effort is complex, costly, or time-consuming. Under the second question, the court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. This entails a five-stage cognitive and operational methodology: the observation of the subject matter of the problem, the formulation of a clear objective, the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, the formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty, and the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses by experiment or analysis.

Under the third question, the court evaluates whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses, thereby disqualifying intuitive trial-and-error tinkering where parameters are altered without causal analysis. Under the fourth question, the court asks whether the process resulted in a technological advancement, or whether the overall approach adopted was aimed at achieving a scientific or technological advancement—defined as an advancement in the general understanding of scientific or technological principles observable to a competent professional in the field, including the decisive rejection of a reasonable hypothesis that proves a particular technological pathway is unfeasible. Finally, under the fifth question, the court asks whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed. Judge Bowman emphasized that because systematic investigation operates within the total discipline of the scientific method, keeping detailed contemporaneous records of hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progresses is an inherent by-product of genuine SR&ED.

The Northwest Hydraulic five-question framework was formally adopted as binding appellate law across Canada by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 5087, and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 D.T.C. 6740. In its current Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy, the CRA consolidates Judge Bowman's five questions into three administrative eligibility criteria—scientific or technological uncertainty, scientific or technological content (systematic investigation), and scientific or technological advancement—while treating the fifth criterion (contemporaneous documentation) as an evidentiary requirement verified in Part 2, Section C of Form T661.
Evolution of Tax Court of Canada Precedents on Routine Engineering, Documentation, and Contract Payments
Subsequent decisions of the Tax Court of Canada have rigorously enforced every prong of the Northwest Hydraulic framework:

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839
Statutory interpretation of "SR&ED" under ITA s. 248(1) in physical hydraulic modelling projects.
Established the canonical five-question test; distinguished technological uncertainty and advancement from "routine engineering".
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 D.T.C. 6740; RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen
Appellate validity of the Northwest Hydraulic five-factor analytical framework.
Elevated Judge Bowman's five questions to settled appellate law binding on all lower courts and CRA auditors.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261 (May 11, 2011)
Whether evaluating geometric shapes for snap-fit closures and material strength-to-weight ratios in moulded plastic storage bins constituted SR&ED.

Appeal dismissed. Held that testing different materials and geometric configurations via standard manufacturing processes without formulating and systematically testing hypotheses to resolve an underlying technological uncertainty is routine product development.
Scope of "contract payment" under ITA s. 127(9) and s. 127(18) where a claimant develops custom technology for an arm's-length corporate customer.

Clarified the distinction between a contract for SR&ED performed "for or on behalf of" a taxable supplier (which is a contract payment that grinds down the performer's qualified expenditures to nil) versus a contract for the sale of a commercial product/deliverable where the performer bears the financial/technical risk and retains its SR&ED claim.
Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42; Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 205
Cumulative nature of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria and evidentiary weight of Criterion 5 (contemporaneous records).

Reaffirmed that "to be eligible for SR&ED, each of the questions in the five-factor test must be answered in the affirmative". While the ITA does not prescribe a specific format of record-keeping, absence of contemporaneous evidence of hypotheses and test results is generally fatal to proving Criteria 2 and 3.
National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (July 7, 2020)
Eligibility of software development ("PTS Project" automating SR&ED claim preparation) lacking contemporaneous records of systematic experimentation.
Appeal dismissed with costs. Developing complex software applications without documented technological uncertainty or contemporaneous test records fails the Northwest Hydraulic standard.
Anne-Marie Chagnon Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 35 (March 24, 2023)
Eligibility of secondary manufacturing operations and mould/tool design projects under ITA s. 248(1).
Appeal dismissed. Confirmed that tool development and process optimization lacking systematic hypothesis testing and contemporaneous documentation do not constitute SR&ED under s. 248(1).

body.text: Statutory Penalty Architecture and Criminal Enforcement

To deter aggressive contingency-fee claim inflation and fraudulent filings, the Income Tax Act enforces a multi-layered civil and criminal penalty regime targeting both claimants and third-party SR&ED claim preparers:

cells: Claimant and Claim Preparer, jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable
False statement or omission in Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information) of Form T661 (missing, incomplete, or inaccurate preparer BN/SIN, fee arrangement, or fee amount).

$1,000 per SR&ED claim. Defence (s. 162(5.2)): A claim preparer is not liable if they exercised the degree of care, diligence, and skill to prevent the false statement or omission that a reasonably prudent person would have exercised in comparable circumstances.
Knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, making, participating in, assenting to, or acquiescing in the making of a false statement or omission in a return or Form T661.

Greater of $100 and 50% of the understated tax and/or overstated SR&ED ITC refund (paragraph 163(2)(d)). Under s. 163(3), the burden of establishing facts justifying the penalty rests on the Minister.

Making, furnishing, participating in, or acquiescing in a false statement that could be used by another person for a tax purpose, with actual knowledge or "culpable conduct" (conduct showing an indifference to compliance with the ITA or a wilful, reckless, or wanton disregard of the law).
$1,000, or for planning/valuation activities the greater of $1,000 and 100% of the planner's gross entitlements from the scheme.

Making, participating in, assenting to, or acquiescing in a false statement to, or by or on behalf of, another person (e.g., fabricating technical narratives on Form T661), with knowledge or culpable conduct.

Greater of $1,000 and the lesser of: (a) the penalty to which the claimant would be liable under subsection 163(2) if the statement were made knowingly, and (b) $100,000 plus the preparer's gross compensation.

Criminal tax evasion / fraud: obtaining or claiming a refundable SR&ED tax credit by making, participating in, or acquiescing in false or deceptive statements or destroying/falsifying books and records.

Summary Conviction: Fine of 50% to 200% of the falsely claimed credit/refund and/or imprisonment up to 2 years. On Indictment (s. 239(2)): Fine of 100% to 200% of the excess credit/refund sought and imprisonment for up to 5 years.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions and Compliance Optimization Framework

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, alongside provincial structural reforms such as Quebec's CRIC consolidation and the CRA's April 1, 2026 Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process, establishes a highly lucrative yet technically demanding compliance environment for Canadian R&D claimants. To maximize non-dilutive tax recovery while insulating claims from reassessment and statutory penalties, corporate tax directors, chief technology officers, and legal counsel must integrate five interconnected compliance protocols into their fiscal governance.

First, qualifying CCPCs and newly eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) scaling their R&D budgets between $3 million and $6 million should model both the expanded $15 million–$75 million taxable capital phase-out and the alternative gross revenue phase-out election. Capital-intensive ventures in clean technology, hardware, robotics, and life sciences that carry high balance-sheet equity or debt should affirmatively elect the gross revenue method on their post-December 15, 2024 T2 filings to preserve full 35% refundability up to $2.1 million annually, while ensuring that corporate association rules under section 256 and Schedule T2SCH49 allocations under subsection 127(10.3) are verified prior to filing.

Second, for depreciable R&D machinery, testing rigs, and prototyping equipment acquired on or after December 16, 2024, taxpayers must document the 90% All or Substantially All (ASA) SR&ED operating-time intent at the exact point of acquisition (or track >50% primary usage for Shared-Use Equipment across the two 12-month terms) and verify the asset's "available-for-use" date under subsection 127(11.2). Simultaneously, multi-provincial filers must account for sub-national divergence: while British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Ontario (for both the OITC and the ORDTC) recognize capital expenditures, Alberta's IEG (AT1 Schedule 29) explicitly restricts post-December 15, 2024 claims to Line 557 current expenditures.

Third, because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under Regulation 2900(4) precludes any separate claim for cloud computing, GPU server rentals, or SaaS subscriptions, artificial intelligence and data-intensive companies whose incremental R&D cloud infrastructure spend exceeds 55% of their direct SR&ED salary base should transition to the Traditional Method. To sustain a Traditional Method claim on audit, engineering teams must deploy dedicated, tagged R&D cloud accounts separated from commercial production workloads.

Fourth, corporations and partnerships with gross business income under $25 million embarking on multi-year R&D programs should utilize the April 1, 2026 Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process to lock in a 3-year technical eligibility ruling within 8 weeks and access the 90-day fast-track expenditure review window. However, because including even a single unapproved project on Form T661 disqualifies the entire annual claim from the 90-day fast track and returns it to the 180-day review queue, claimants must strictly align their claimed project portfolio with their pre-approved submissions.

Finally, technical narratives in Part 2 of Form T661 must be anchored in real-time engineering artifacts—such as source-code version logs, issue-tracking tickets, experimental test logs, failed hypothesis analyses, and contemporaneous weekly timesheets—generated as the work progressed to satisfy Criterion 5 of Northwest Hydraulic. On the financial side, corporate controllers must verify that all accrued SR&ED salaries and subcontractor invoices are disbursed within 180 days of fiscal year-end to avoid disallowance under subsections 78(4) and 127(26), verify Part 9 claim preparer disclosures to prevent subsection 162(5.1) penalties, and file complete T661 and provincial schedules well ahead of the non-extendable 18-month statutory bar under subsections 37(11) and 220(2.2).
